```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                     fig.align = "center", dpi = 120)
raiz <- normalizePath(if (file.exists("R/02_regresiones_por_modelo.R")) "." else "..")
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = raiz)
e <- new.env(parent = globalenv())
op <- options(correr_02 = FALSE)
tryCatch(sys.source(file.path(raiz, "R/02_regresiones_por_modelo.R"), envir = e),
         finally = options(op))
base <- e$cargar_base(file.path(raiz, e$in_file))
datos <- e$preparar_respuesta(base, politica = "medio_punto")
ajustes <- e$ajustar_modelos(datos, lambda = 0)
coeficientes <- e$tabla_coeficientes(ajustes)
eval <- read.csv(file.path(raiz, "R/resultados/evaluacion.csv"))
principal <- eval[eval$method == "regressions_48_half_point", ]
baseline_bt <- eval[eval$method == "general_bradley_terry", ]
baseline_wr <- eval[eval$method == "general_win_rate_half_point", ]
stopifnot(nrow(principal) == 1L, nrow(baseline_bt) == 1L,
          nrow(baseline_wr) == 1L, length(ajustes) == 48L)
chico <- names(ajustes)[which.min(vapply(ajustes, function(x) x$n_votos, numeric(1)))]
escenarios <- list(Code = "is_code", Math = "math",
  `Creative writing` = "creative_writing",
  Instructions = "instruction_following", `Code + math` = c("is_code", "math"),
  `All questions` = character())
```

## What I did

I updated Jaime's existing regressions to use the group's November 2 decisions.
Each AI model has one regression. A question can have several features at once.
The model estimates an **expected preference score**: win = 1, loss = 0,
and tie or both bad = 0.5. With half points, this score is not simply the
probability of winning a decisive vote.

The descriptive fit below uses **`r format(nrow(datos)/2, big.mark=",")` votes**
from April through July, represented by two model-side rows per vote.
There are `r length(ajustes)` fitted models. As in Jaime's original code,
flagged review cases are excluded from the fit. The original data are unchanged.

## Response and predictors

The response is the model's score for that vote. These are the only predictors;
all describe the question, before the AI writes an answer.

```{r features}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Feature = e$predictores,
  Meaning = c("The question involves programming.",
    "The question involves mathematics.",
    "The question asks for creative writing.",
    "The question contains specific instructions.",
    "The question is complex.",
    "The task needs creative thinking.",
    "The task needs subject knowledge.",
    "The task needs problem-solving steps.",
    "The task has a practical, real-world use.",
    "The task is specific and well defined.",
    "The task needs technical accuracy.")), row.names = FALSE)
```

Response length, formatting, price and tokens are **not** predictors.
The opponent is not a predictor in these separate regressions (group decision 5).

This is the actual regression specification:

```{r glm-visible, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
glm(y ~ is_code + math + creative_writing + instruction_following +
      complexity + creativity + domain_knowledge + problem_solving +
      real_world + specificity + technical_accuracy,
    family = quasibinomial(), data = votes_for_one_model)
```

The default uses `lambda = 0`, so these are ordinary `glm()` fits. The updated
function also accepts ridge: `ajustar_modelos(datos, lambda = ...)`. It shrinks
only the 11 feature effects, never the intercept. **Mark will choose lambda
using train only**; this report does not choose it by looking at July.

## The regressions: full R output

A positive `math` coefficient means a higher fitted preference score on math
questions, holding the other features fixed. It is a change in log-odds, not a
percentage-point change or a causal effect. For example, Gemini's math
coefficient is **`r round(coef(ajustes[["gemini-2.5-pro"]])["mathTRUE"], 3)`**.
P-values below are nominal: the rows are not independent across models.

Open each example to see its **complete `summary()` output**, including
coefficients, dispersion and convergence information. The third example has
the fewest votes in this descriptive fit.

```{r summaries, results='asis'}
for (modelo in c("gemini-2.5-pro", "claude-opus-4-20250514", chico)) {
  cat(sprintf("<details><summary>%s — %s votes</summary>\n", modelo,
              format(ajustes[[modelo]]$n_votos, big.mark = ",")))
  cat(sprintf('<p><code>summary(ajustes[["%s"]])</code></p>\n', modelo))
  texto <- paste(capture.output(print(summary(ajustes[[modelo]]))), collapse = "\n")
  cat("<pre>", htmltools::htmlEscape(texto), "</pre></details>\n")
}
```

## Feature effects for all 48 models

Blue means a higher preference score when a feature is present; red means a
lower score. These are **log-odds coefficients**, with the other features held
fixed. The intercept is omitted from this chart. Full values, including all
intercepts, are in `R/resultados/coeficientes_por_modelo.csv`.

```{r heatmap, fig.width=11, fig.height=12, out.width='100%', fig.cap='Descriptive fit: all April–July votes, half points, no ridge.'}
mapa <- coeficientes[coeficientes$termino != "(Intercept)", ]
mapa$feature <- sub("TRUE$", "", mapa$termino)
mapa$feature <- factor(mapa$feature, levels = e$predictores)
mapa$modelo <- factor(mapa$modelo, levels = rev(sort(unique(mapa$modelo))))
ggplot2::ggplot(mapa, ggplot2::aes(feature, modelo, fill = estimado)) +
  ggplot2::geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#b64c3c", mid = "#f7f9fb",
                               high = "#22679c", midpoint = 0) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Log-odds") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  ggplot2::theme(panel.grid = ggplot2::element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = ggplot2::element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    axis.text.y = ggplot2::element_text(size = 8))
```

## Does it predict unseen votes?

The descriptive fit above uses all months and is **not** a test result.
The table below comes directly from **Mark's saved evaluation**. Mark fits
on April–June only and evaluates decisive July votes where both models were
seen in train. Ties and both bad affect the half-point training fit but are
not scored as winners in the test.

```{r evaluation}
comparacion <- rbind(baseline_bt, baseline_wr, principal)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Method = c("General Bradley–Terry ranking (decisive train votes)",
    "General win rate (half points in train)",
    "Separate regressions (half points in train)"),
  `July votes` = comparacion$test_votes_evaluated,
  Correct = comparacion$correct,
  `Accuracy (%)` = comparacion$accuracy_percent,
  `Log-loss (lower is better)` = comparacion$logloss,
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE, digits = 4)
```

The separate regressions gain **`r round(100 * (principal$correct - baseline_bt$correct) / principal$test_votes_evaluated, 2)`
percentage points** in accuracy over the general Bradley–Terry ranking: a small
improvement. Their log-loss is clearly better than the general win rate.
Against Bradley–Terry, the log-loss difference is small and Mark's interval
reaches zero; we cannot claim a clear improvement in probability quality.
These statements follow the correction in `docs/12-decisiones-2-11.md`.

## Top 3 by task

`top3()` averages fitted scores over **real questions** with each feature,
allowing the other features to vary. Here the descriptive fit uses all months.
Only models with **at least 100 votes in July** can be recommended. Versions
remain separate. These are task recommendations, not a new test evaluation.

```{r recommendations}
tabla_top <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(escenarios), function(nombre) {
  t <- e$top3(escenarios[[nombre]], ajustes)
  data.frame(Task = nombre, Rank = t$rank, Model = t$modelo,
             `Preference score` = round(t$prob_ganar, 3),
             check.names = FALSE)
}))
knitr::kable(tabla_top, row.names = FALSE)
```

An optional budget filters **output price per million tokens**, not total
cost per answer. Unknown prices are excluded only when a budget is supplied.
For example:

```{r budget-code, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
top3("math", ajustes, precio_max = 2)
```

## Limits and next step

- Each vote contributes two model-side rows; the separate fits are dependent.
- The main test is one time split, April–June versus July.
- Four models appear only in July and cannot be tested with that training set.

The combined Bradley–Terry model is a separate next task. It will use one row
per vote and account directly for the opponent. This report does not include it.
